rows.title: Policy
rows.figure: RBNZ held 2.75% (4–3) vs ~85–95% hike priced; RBA Nov 3 hike ~79–85% (from ~50–60%); BoC today hike ~78–85%; Fed today hold ~91%, Dec hike ~73–82%; ECB Oct 29 hold ~95%; BoJ Oct 30 hold ~98%; BoE Nov 5 hike ~90–97%
rows.read: New Zealand's central bank surprised markets by holding rates, though it still expects to hike later, while hot inflation in Australia made a November hike there likely. Today Canada and the Fed decide, and for both the signal about what comes next matters more than the decision. Most banks still lean toward hikes because energy keeps inflation high.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US consumer confidence Oct 91.7 (fc 81.2); durable goods Sep +1.8%; US Q3 GDP Thu fc 3.0% annualised; euro-area Q3 GDP Fri
rows.read: There was no major growth news overnight, so the picture is unchanged: a strong US economy against a soft euro area and a weak Australian jobs market. That gap keeps favouring the dollar. US growth figures on Thursday are the next big check.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Australia Q3 trimmed CPI +1.0% q/q (RBA fc 0.8%); headline Sep 4.3% y/y (fc 4.2%); Tokyo CPI tonight 6:30 PM CT; US PCE Thu 7:30 AM CT (core fc +0.3% m/m)
rows.read: Australian inflation ran hotter than its central bank expected, the latest sign that high energy costs are feeding into prices. That keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes, which supports currencies whose banks act. The US inflation measure the Fed watches most comes on Thursday.

rows.figure: Nikkei +1.2%, KOSPI >+3% (Oct 28 Asia); USD/JPY ~157.8; USD/CHF ~0.830; Israel count ~42%: no bloc near 61 seats; shekel ~−1%
rows.read: Asian stocks rallied on strong chipmaker results, so markets stayed calm and the yen and franc drew little safety demand. Israel's election produced no clear winner, which hit the shekel but not the major currencies. The Fed's tone this afternoon is the main risk to that calm.

rows.title: Terms of trade
rows.figure: Brent $115.36 (+1.3%); WTI $101.12 (+1.2%); Ras Tanura claim unconfirmed; API crude −2.0M bbl; OPEC+ meets Sunday
rows.read: Oil rose again as hopes for the Iran talks faded and Saudi Arabia stayed silent on a claimed refinery strike. That helps exporters like Canada and Australia and costs importers like Japan and the euro area. Until the talks produce terms, the war premium stays in the price.

rows.figure: CFTC Oct 20: funds strongly against CAD (sharply added), against NZD (sharply added) and EUR (added), for GBP (real money strongly against), for AUD (real money strongly against), leaning against JPY, strongly for gold
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, so a Bank of Canada hike with a signal of more today could force them to buy it back. Their bets against the kiwi paid off overnight. In the pound and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: UK Budget today ~7:30 AM CT; dealer poll: 2026-27 gilt sales +£3.4bn to £249.6bn; French revenue vote Nov 3; France–Germany 10-year gap ~167 bp
rows.read: Chancellor John Healey presents his first UK Budget this morning, and dealers expect only a small rise in government bond sales. Borrowing close to that would keep UK bonds calm; a bigger jump could unsettle them and the pound. France's budget vote is still delayed, which keeps a weight on the euro.
